claims.claim: Le Guin praises Tolkien's plain English for ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: Le Guin faults the failed fantasy style for sensory cues so vague that the rocks, wind and trees are not felt.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: the rocks, the wind, the trees are not there

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies the prose style she is attacking as journalistic prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: To what then is it appropriate? To journalism.

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in journalism the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate

claims.claim: Le Guin asserts that speech expresses character, whether or not the writer intends it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.page: p.4, after the three dialogue samples

claims.claim: Le Guin defines the musical dimension of prose as the sound of the words, the movement of the syntax and the rhythm of the sentences.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences

claims.claim: Le Guin reports that the Song of Roland has four thousand lines containing one simile and no metaphors.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the archaic manner a trap into which almost all very young fantasy writers walk.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: a trap into which almost all very young fantasy writers walk

claims.claim: Le Guin notes approvingly that Jack Vance's achieved style contains no archaisms at all.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: And it contains no archaisms at all.

claims.claim: Le Guin dismisses imitation Dunsany as made-up names plus a great many sentences beginning with 'And'.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: a great many sentences beginning with

claims.claim: Le Guin says that alternating colloquial American English with old formal usages makes characters lose coherence for her as a reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: the characters lose coherence in my mind

claims.claim: Le Guin asserts that style is not an ingredient added to a book but is the book itself.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1972 speech; Pendragon Press 1973)
claims.quote: The style, of course, is the book.

claims.claim: Le Guin opens her writing guide by saying the sound of the language is where it all begins.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised ed.), chapter 1, excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins.
claims.page: Steering the Craft ch.1, first line

claims.claim: Le Guin makes the test of a sentence whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised ed.), chapter 1, excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?
claims.page: Steering the Craft ch.1, first paragraph

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular, unlike those of poetry.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised ed.), chapter 1, excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular
claims.page: Steering the Craft ch.1, first paragraph

verdicts.trueWording: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately
verdicts.note: Exact on p.8 of the raw PDF: "Tolkien writes a plain, clear English. Its outstanding virtue is its flexibility, its variety. It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately..." The praise limb is carried by "outstanding virtue".

verdicts.trueWording: the rocks, the wind, the trees are not there, are not felt
verdicts.note: Exact on p.8: "Its sensory cues--extremely important in imaginative writing--are vague and generalized; the rocks, the wind, the trees are not there, are not felt." The subject is explicitly "the Poughkeepsie style of fantasy", the style she names as the one she is attacking.

verdicts.trueWording: To what then is it appropriate? To journalism. It is journalistic prose.
verdicts.note: Exact on p.8, immediately after "the kind of writing I am attacking, the Poughkeepsie style of fantasy", so the attacking limb is supported in the same paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: In journalism, the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate
verdicts.note: Exact on p.8; the quoted clause is preceded on the page by "In journalism,", which supplies the claim's "in journalism" limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: Speech expresses character. It does so whether the speaker or the author knows it or not.
verdicts.note: Exact on p.4, directly after the third dialogue sample, as cited. Wording caveat: the page says "whether the speaker or the author KNOWS it or not", not "intends"; unintended is entailed by unknown, so the limb holds, but the source's axis is knowledge, not intention.

verdicts.trueWording: in the sound of the words, the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences
verdicts.note: Exact on p.6, in the appraisal of Eddison's prose: "musically--that is, in the sound of the words, the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences--it is subtle and very strong." The "that is" makes it an explicit gloss, i.e. a definition.

verdicts.trueWording: The Song of Roland has four thousand lines, containing one simile and no metaphors
verdicts.note: Exact on p.8, in the passage on epic plainness ("Most epics are in straightforward language... A plain language is the noblest of all").

verdicts.trueWording: It is a trap into which almost all very young fantasy writers walk
verdicts.note: Exact on p.5; the antecedent in the preceding sentence is "archaicizing, the archaic manner", so the claim's subject limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: It is an achieved style. And it contains no archaisms at all.
verdicts.note: Exact at the foot of p.7, closing the Jack Vance paragraph. The approving limb is supported by the surrounding praise ("how very good a writer he is"; "clear, graceful, and precisely suited").

verdicts.trueWording: elaborate made-up names... and a great many sentences beginning with "And."
verdicts.note: Exact on p.5. Completeness caveat: Le Guin's list has three items, not two - the claim omits "some vague descriptions of gorgeous cities and unmentionable dooms". Both limbs it does assert are on the page, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: the characters lose coherence in my mind, and I lose confidence in them
verdicts.note: Exact on p.7, on Leiber and Zelazny, who "alternate the two styles": colloquial American English for humor, "old formal usages" at earnest moments. Every limb, including the first-person reader stance, is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: The style, of course, is the book.
verdicts.note: Exact on p.9, answering the preceding sentence about editors who treat style "as if it were an ingredient of a book... or something added onto the book", which supports the claim's "not an ingredient added to a book" limb.

verdicts.trueWording: The sound of the language is where it all begins.
verdicts.note: Exact and page-initial in the excerpt body. The page's own standfirst states it is "the first chapter of Ursula K. Le Guin's updated edition of Steering the Craft", supporting both the "opens" and "her writing guide" limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?
verdicts.note: Exact, the second sentence of the chapter's first paragraph, as cited.

verdicts.trueWording: though the sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular
verdicts.note: Exact in the first paragraph. Contrast caveat: the poetry limb rests on the concessive full sentence - "This is just as true of prose as it is of poetry, though the sound effects of prose are usually subtle and always irregular" - so the difference from poetry is conceded by "though" rather than asserted about poetry outright.
